newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to meet aspiring members in pessimistic mood.
newsitem.headline: EU to meet aspiring members in pessimistic mood.

text.p: The European Union meets leaders from aspiring member countries on Friday, aware that its plans to prepare the bloc for the day it has up to a dozen new members are far from cut and dried.

At a special meeting in Amsterdam to brief 10 eastern European countries, Cyprus and Turkey on the outcome of last week's Amsterdam summit, the EU will have to admit that internal reforms to prepare for enlargement have simply not been done.

In a hint of the pessimistic mood in which the EU side will approach the meeting, European Commission President Jacques Santer told the European Parliament on Thursday the failure did not bode well for the EU's eastern expansion project.

"I do not think this augurs well for enlargement," he said in a report on the summit, which agreed to defer a decision on how to reform the EU institutions, originally set up for six members, until the time of the expansion.

"I do not want to see a situation whereby on the eve of enlargement we are forced to say to our future members 'You have done everything to prepare yourselves for entering the EU. Unfortunately the EU hasn't been able to get ready to receive you'."
An equally dispirited Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, who will host Friday's meeting, said he hoped the EU could show more political will at the time of the enlargement itself.

A wave of excitement has been mounting in 10 central and eastern European countries as the European Commission prepares to unveil on July 16 its advice to EU governments on how suitable each is for EU entry.
At the same time it will indicate in what areas, notably farming and financing, EU policy reforms will be needed.
The European Commissioner reponsible for enlargement, Hans van den Broek, told reporters on Wednesday he was receiving daily inquiries about who would match up and who would not.

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Romania, Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are all in the queue for the EU's eastwards expansion and anxiously waiting to see whether the bloc will decide to open talks with all of them at the same time, or on a staggered basis.
Talks with Cyprus will start early next year.

Turkey, whose EU membership bid has been shunned by the European Commission on human rights grounds, has been invited to the Amsterdam meeting in a growing sign that the EU wants its strategically placed neighbour to feel part of the European picture.

Although the EU leaders' failure to agree internal reforms is not expected to have an impact on the opening of talks, it could delay the day the aspirants cross the EU's threshold, a date which has increasingly retreated into the distance.

A Commission spokesman told reporters on Thursday there was general agreement among EU members that the expansion could not proceed until the reform of the EU's decision-making procedures had been agreed.
